title: What is the PACELC theorem and how does it extend CAP: during a network Partition choose Availability or Consistency (same as CAP), but Else (when the system is running normally with no partition) you still face a trade-off between Latency and Consistency: and why does this matter (CAP only talks about failure mode, but most of the time the system is healthy and the real daily trade-off is "do I wait for all replicas to ack (consistent but slower) or return after one ack (fast but possibly stale)"): e.g. DynamoDB is PA/EL (available during partition, low-latency normally), PostgreSQL synchronous replication is PC/EC (consistent always, at the cost of latency)?
shortTitle: PACELC Theorem: Extending CAP to the Healthy-System Case

s1_definition.oneliner: PACELC says: during a Partition choose A or C (like CAP), Else during normal operation choose Latency or Consistency: it covers the healthy case CAP ignores.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CAP blind spot** – CAP only describes behavior during a network partition, which is the rare failure mode.
- **PACELC extension** – if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normally), choose Latency or Consistency.
- **Two-letter label** – a system is classified as PA/EL, PC/EC, etc., describing behavior in both regimes.
- **Everyday trade-off** – even with a healthy network, writes must decide how many replica acks to wait for before responding.
- **Per-operation tuning** – balance writes can be EC while feed reads can be EL, tuned per query.
s1_definition.analogy: CAP only describes what National Bank of India does when the phone line between branches breaks. But the line is fine almost all the time, and even then there is a choice: when Rajesh updates his balance, do the branches wait until every branch confirms before telling him "done" (consistent but slower), or does the nearest branch say "done" immediately and tell the others later (fast but briefly stale)? PACELC adds that everyday trade-off.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
           ┌──────────────────────────────┐
           │        PACELC Theorem         │
           └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                          │
              ┌───────────┴───────────┐
              ▼                       ▼
     ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐
     │ If Partition (P) │    │ Else (E)         │
     │ Choose:          │    │ Choose:          │
     │  A: Available    │    │  L: Low Latency  │
     │  C: Consistent   │    │  C: Consistent   │
     └────────┬────────┘    └────────┬────────┘
              │                      │
     ┌────────┴────────┐    ┌────────┴────────┐
     │ PA: DynamoDB     │    │ EL: DynamoDB     │
     │ PC: PostgreSQL   │    │ EC: PostgreSQL   │
     └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘

     DynamoDB: PA/EL  (fast, eventually consistent)
     PostgreSQL sync: PC/EC (correct, higher latency)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
PACELC extends CAP by covering the normal-operation case that CAP ignores. It says: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency (which is exactly CAP); Else, when the network is healthy, choose Latency or Consistency. A system is labeled with two letters like PA/EL or PC/EC.

The Else half matters because partitions are rare but every single write faces the "wait for all acks or return after one" question. This everyday latency-versus-staleness decision dominates p99 latency and read-your-writes behavior. CAP-only thinking fixates on the rare failure case.

Concretely, PostgreSQL with synchronous replication is PC/EC (consistent always, at the cost of latency) while DynamoDB is PA/EL (available during partition, low-latency normally with eventually-consistent reads). At the National Bank of India, Pankaj classifies per operation: balance writes are EC so a read after a write is always correct, while feed and counter writes are EL for speed with brief acceptable staleness.

Remember one sentence: during a partition choose A or C like CAP, else choose latency or consistency, and apply it per operation: EC for money, EL for feeds.

---

keyPoints: CAP only describes behavior during a network partition; PACELC adds the healthy-system trade-off.
During a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.
A system is labeled with two choices: PA/EL (DynamoDB default), PC/EC (PostgreSQL sync replication).
The Else trade-off (wait for replicas or ack fast) dominates daily p99 latency and read-your-writes behavior.
PACELC should be applied per operation: EC for financial data, EL for feeds and counters.
Cassandra and DynamoDB expose this as tunable consistency levels per request (ONE vs QUORUM).
EL for balance writes can cause stale reads, which is unacceptable for money.
